Sunlight looks white, but it’s actually a mixture of many colors, from red and orange to blue and violet. You can see these colors when a prism splits sunlight into a rainbow.

Light travels in waves, and different colors have different wavelengths. Blue light has shorter waves than red light.

As sunlight enters Earth’s atmosphere, it bumps into tiny molecules of gases such as nitrogen and oxygen. These molecules scatter light in all directions. But they scatter short-wavelength blue light much more strongly than long-wavelength red light. So, wherever you look in the sky, lots of scattered blue light reaches your eyes.

This effect is called **Rayleigh scattering**.

You might wonder: if violet light has an even shorter wavelength, why isn’t the sky violet? Sunlight contains less violet light, our eyes are less sensitive to it, and some violet is absorbed high in the atmosphere. Together, these effects make the sky look blue.

At sunrise and sunset, sunlight travels through more atmosphere before reaching you. Much of the blue light is scattered away along the way, leaving more red and orange light to reach your eyes.

In space, there’s almost no atmosphere to scatter sunlight, so the sky looks black—even when the Sun is shining.

The sky looks blue because of the way sunlight interacts with the air around Earth.

A **browser cache** is a temporary storage area where your browser keeps copies of files from websites you visit. These can include images, fonts, stylesheets, scripts, and sometimes entire pages.

Imagine visiting a news website. The first time, your browser downloads the site’s logo and other files from the website’s server. It may save some of those files in its cache. When you visit again, the browser can reuse the saved copies instead of downloading everything again.

This makes pages load faster, reduces data usage, and puts less demand on the website’s server.

Websites send instructions that help the browser decide **what can be cached and for how long**. Once a cached copy is considered old, the browser may ask the server whether it has changed. If it hasn’t, the browser can keep using the saved copy; if it has, the browser downloads the newer version.

Sometimes a cached file can cause a page to look outdated or behave unexpectedly. Refreshing the page may help, and clearing the cache forces the browser to download fresh copies. However, the next visit may be slower because the browser has to rebuild its cache.

A cache isn’t a complete offline copy of the web: many pages still need an internet connection.

The phone was ringing when Mara found it among the rocks below the lighthouse. It lay in a pool of seawater, its black screen lighting the shells around it like a tiny green moon.

She had come down to check the storm damage. Three steps from the bottom of the path, she had heard the sound: a bright, impatient trill that belonged to kitchens and train stations, not this empty coast.

It stopped as she reached for it.

Mara lifted the phone. No water dripped from it. The glass was warm.

On the screen, a single word appeared:

HOME.

The phone rang again.

She looked up at the lighthouse. Its lantern was dark in the gray morning, but someone stood behind the glass.

Mara lived alone. The supply boat was not due until Friday, and the path from the mainland had vanished under the tide at dawn.

The figure raised a hand.

The phone continued to ring.

Mara pressed it to her ear.

“Don’t turn on the light tonight,” said her own voice.

Then the figure in the lantern room waved, and Mara saw that it was holding another phone.

Behind it, the lamp began to turn.

It was noon.

The phone began ringing at low tide, when Mara was halfway down the cliff steps with a bucket of kitchen scraps.

At first she thought the sound was a gull, strangled and insistent. Then it rang again, a bright old-fashioned trill that belonged in a hallway, not among the black rocks below the lighthouse.

She found it wedged in a pool beneath a fringe of bladderwrack. It was a red telephone with a curled cord and no visible connection to anything. Seawater lapped over its base. The receiver trembled with each ring.

Mara set down the bucket. Her father had kept the light before her, and he had taught her that the sea returned what it wanted, when it wanted. Usually, he had been talking about bodies.

The phone stopped.

A wave hissed through the stones. Far above, the lamp turned behind its glass, though daylight had not yet entirely gone.

Then the ringing started again.

Mara lifted the receiver. It was warm against her ear.

“Hello?”

For a moment she heard only breathing and the faint clatter of dishes. Then a man’s voice said, “Mara, don’t let the light go out tonight.”

Her father had been dead eleven years.

One year into engineering management, I’ve learned that the job isn’t about having all the answers. It’s about creating the conditions for a team to find them together.

A few lessons I’m taking into year two:

• **Listen before solving.** Sometimes people need a sounding board, not a solution.

• **Clarity is kindness.** Clear priorities, expectations, and feedback make work better for everyone.

• **Your calendar reflects your priorities.** If coaching and team health matter, make time for them.

• **Delegation is a form of trust.** Giving people ownership means giving them room to make decisions—and learn.

• **Technical work still matters.** You may write less code, but you need enough context to ask good questions and support sound decisions.

• **Celebrate progress.** It’s easy to move straight to the next problem. Pause to recognize the people who got you this far.

I’m grateful to the teammates and mentors who made the first year a learning experience.

**Pride and Prejudice** by Jane Austen follows Elizabeth Bennet, one of five sisters in a family whose estate will pass to a male relative when their father dies. Because the sisters have limited financial prospects, their mother is eager to see them married.

Elizabeth meets the wealthy Mr. Darcy, whose apparent arrogance and dismissive behavior lead her to dislike him. Her prejudice deepens when the charming officer George Wickham tells her that Darcy has treated him unjustly. Meanwhile, Elizabeth’s sister Jane falls in love with Darcy’s friend Mr. Bingley, but the couple is separated, partly through Darcy’s intervention.

When Darcy proposes to Elizabeth, she rejects him, accusing him of pride and cruelty. He then explains his actions in a letter, revealing Wickham’s dishonesty. As Elizabeth revises her judgments, Darcy also changes, becoming more considerate and helping rescue her family from scandal after Wickham elopes with her youngest sister. Elizabeth and Darcy eventually recognize their love and marry, while Jane reunites with Bingley.

The novel explores how pride and prejudice distort perception, and how self-knowledge makes personal growth possible. It also examines the pressures of class, wealth, and marriage in a society where women’s security often depends on finding a husband.

**Pride and Prejudice by Jane Austen**

Elizabeth Bennet is one of five sisters whose future security depends largely on marriage. When the wealthy Mr. Bingley rents a nearby estate, he falls in love with Elizabeth’s gentle elder sister, Jane. His friend Mr. Darcy, however, seems arrogant and dismissive, particularly toward Elizabeth.

Elizabeth’s dislike of Darcy deepens when the charming officer Mr. Wickham claims that Darcy treated him unfairly. Darcy later proposes to Elizabeth, but she rejects him, accusing him of arrogance and of separating Jane from Bingley. In a letter, Darcy explains his actions and reveals that Wickham is dishonest.

As Elizabeth reconsiders her judgments, she discovers Darcy’s generosity and loyalty. When her younger sister Lydia elopes with Wickham, Darcy quietly intervenes to arrange their marriage, protecting the Bennet family from scandal. Bingley returns and proposes to Jane. Darcy and Elizabeth eventually acknowledge their changed feelings and become engaged.

The novel explores how pride and prejudice distort perception, while showing that self-knowledge can make love possible. It also examines the pressure on women to marry for financial security and exposes the absurdities of a society governed by wealth, rank, and reputation. Austen treats these serious concerns with wit, irony, and affection for her flawed characters.

The printing press changed Europe by making written information faster and cheaper to reproduce. Before its spread, books were usually copied by hand, making them expensive and scarce. In the mid-fifteenth century, Johannes Gutenberg combined movable metal type with a mechanical press to produce books on a much larger scale. Printing had existed in East Asia for centuries, but its expansion in Europe had far-reaching effects.

More books meant that scholars, merchants and eventually a wider public could share ideas across greater distances. Printing helped spread Renaissance learning and encouraged the use of vernacular languages alongside Latin. Although literacy grew gradually rather than overnight, printed materials gave people more reasons and opportunities to learn to read.

The press also transformed religious debate. Martin Luther’s writings were printed and distributed widely, helping the Protestant Reformation challenge the authority of the Catholic Church. Religious leaders used print to defend their beliefs, while governments tried to censor works they considered dangerous.

In science, printed diagrams, data and arguments could be checked, criticized and built upon by researchers in different places. Printing also supported trade through maps, manuals and news. It did not create agreement: false claims and propaganda spread too. But by multiplying access to information, the press reshaped European culture, religion, politics and knowledge.

The printing press changed Europe by making written information much cheaper and faster to produce. In the mid fifteenth century, Johannes Gutenberg developed a European printing system using movable metal type. Before then, most books were copied by hand, a slow and expensive process. Printing made it possible to produce hundreds of copies of a text in the time previously needed to copy one.

As books became more available, more people had reason and opportunity to learn to read. Printers published not only religious works in Latin but also books in languages such as English, French and German. This helped spread common written forms of those languages and allowed ideas to reach readers beyond scholars and clergy.

Printing also transformed religious debate. After Martin Luther challenged Church practices in 1517, printed pamphlets carried his arguments across Europe. His supporters and opponents used the press to rally audiences, helping fuel the Protestant Reformation.

Scientists and scholars benefited too. They could share findings more widely, compare evidence and build on one another’s work. At the same time, rulers and religious authorities tried to censor publications they considered dangerous.

The effects were gradual and uneven, but printing changed who could access knowledge and how quickly ideas could travel.

Instead of canceling my plans, I borrowed an umbrella and stepped into streets shining beneath a silver sky. At a North Beach café, I warmed my hands around a cappuccino and watched umbrellas bob past the window. The hills disappeared into mist, and the familiar cable cars emerged from it with a cheerful clatter. By late morning, I had wandered to the Ferry Building, where the scent of fresh bread mingled with salty air. I sampled local cheese, bought a still-warm pastry, and lingered over stalls piled high with mushrooms and flowers. Outside, rain blurred the Bay Bridge into a watercolor, but the waterfront was beautiful precisely because it felt so quiet. Later, I ducked into a bookstore in the Mission, then found a taqueria where a steaming burrito made the weather seem like an excellent excuse to slow down. As evening settled, streetlights glowed in puddles and strangers shared awnings while waiting for the rain to ease. I returned to my hotel with damp shoes, a full stomach, and the feeling that I had met the city on its own terms.

Rain turned San Francisco into a watercolor the morning I stepped off the cable car at Powell Street. Mist blurred the hills, and umbrellas bobbed along the sidewalks like bright little boats. I ducked into a coffee shop for a cappuccino and watched raindrops race down the window while commuters hurried past in slick jackets. When the shower softened, I wandered through Chinatown, where red lanterns glowed against the gray sky and the scent of roasted duck drifted from restaurant doors. A warm sesame bun made the perfect companion for the walk toward North Beach, its bakeries fogging their windows with fragrant steam. By afternoon, the rain had returned in earnest, so I found shelter among the shelves of City Lights Bookstore. There is something wonderfully fitting about reading poetry while a storm taps at the glass. Later, I rode a bus to the waterfront and watched ferries disappear into the mist. The Bay Bridge appeared only in fragments, its lights shimmering on dark water. For dinner, a bowl of clam chowder warmed my hands and my spirits. San Francisco may be famous for its views, but on this rainy day, its quieter charms were more than enough for me.

The ramen here is worth considering for the broth alone. Deeply savory, richly layered, and beautifully balanced, it tastes as though it has simmered patiently for hours. The noodles have a pleasing chew, while the toppings are fresh and thoughtfully prepared. A soft-boiled egg adds welcome creaminess, and the slices of pork are tender without overwhelming the bowl.

Unfortunately, the service struggles to match the kitchen’s quality. On my visit, it took a long time to be seated, and the wait for food felt even longer. Staff members were courteous when available, but checking in on tables seemed inconsistent. If you arrive hungry or on a tight schedule, the delays may test your patience.

Still, the comforting, flavorful ramen makes a strong case for a return visit. Come when you have time to spare, settle in, and let that excellent broth be the highlight of an otherwise uneven dining experience.

Remote work can help junior engineers, but only when companies deliberately replace the informal learning that offices often provide. Its greatest advantage is access: a new engineer can join a strong team without relocating, avoid a draining commute, and arrange focused time around personal responsibilities. Remote environments can also encourage clearer written documentation, giving newcomers a searchable record of decisions and procedures. However, beginners frequently learn by overhearing conversations, watching colleagues troubleshoot, and asking small questions before confusion becomes frustration. Those opportunities do not automatically survive a move online. A junior engineer who hesitates to interrupt a busy teammate may spend hours stuck or quietly lose confidence. The solution is not necessarily a mandatory return to the office; it is intentional support. Teams should pair newcomers with mentors, schedule regular check-ins, review code constructively, and make it clear that asking for help is expected. Occasional in-person gatherings can strengthen relationships when practical, but proximity alone does not guarantee good mentorship. Ultimately, remote work helps junior engineers when managers invest in teaching and inclusion; without that investment, flexibility can become isolation. The question is less where beginners sit than whether they have access to guidance, feedback, and meaningful opportunities to grow.

Remote work can help junior engineers, but only when employers deliberately replace the informal learning that happens in an office. Early in their careers, engineers need more than assigned tasks; they need examples of good judgment, frequent feedback, and opportunities to ask seemingly small questions. In a poorly managed remote team, those opportunities can disappear. A newcomer may spend hours stuck because sending a message feels more intrusive than turning to a colleague. They may also miss conversations that explain why technical decisions were made. Yet remote work offers real advantages. It expands access to jobs beyond expensive cities, saves commuting time, and can give beginners quiet space to concentrate. Written discussions and documented decisions can also make knowledge easier to revisit. The crucial factor is not location but support. Teams should provide regular mentoring, pair programming, clear documentation, and explicit invitations to ask for help. Managers should check progress without treating silence as proof that everything is fine. Occasional in person gatherings can strengthen relationships, although they should not substitute for daily guidance. In my view, remote work helps junior engineers when companies invest in teaching; without that investment, flexibility can become isolation and slow their professional growth significantly.

Running and swimming are both effective ways to stay fit, but they place different demands on the body and suit different preferences.

Running is convenient and relatively inexpensive: a suitable pair of shoes and a safe route are often all you need. It strengthens the heart and lungs, works the lower body, and supports bone health because it is a weight-bearing activity. However, its repetitive impact can aggravate joint pain or lead to overuse injuries, especially if distance or speed increases too quickly.

Swimming also improves cardiovascular fitness, while engaging muscles throughout the body, including the shoulders, back, core, and legs. Because water supports much of your weight, swimming is generally gentler on the joints and can be a good option for people who find impact exercise uncomfortable. On the other hand, it requires access to a pool or suitable open water, and learning efficient technique can take time. It also does less to strengthen bones than weight-bearing exercise.

Both activities can be adapted to different fitness levels by changing the pace, duration, or intensity. The best choice is often the one you enjoy and can do regularly. Combining them can also add variety while balancing running’s bone-strengthening benefits with swimming’s lower-impact, full-body workout.

Running and swimming are both effective ways to improve cardiovascular fitness, build endurance, and support overall health. The better choice depends on your goals, physical condition, and preferences.

Running is convenient and relatively inexpensive. A suitable pair of shoes and a safe place to run are usually enough to get started. It strengthens the legs and, because it is a weight bearing activity, can help maintain bone density. However, the repeated impact may aggravate joint problems or lead to overuse injuries if training increases too quickly.

Swimming provides a workout with much less impact on the joints. It engages the arms, shoulders, back, core, and legs, making it a good option for people who want a full body workout or need a gentler activity. Water also provides resistance, which helps develop muscular endurance. Swimming requires access to a pool or suitable open water, though, and good technique can take time to learn. Unlike running, it does relatively little to strengthen bones through weight bearing.

Both activities can be adjusted to suit different fitness levels, from easy sessions to demanding intervals. Choosing the one you enjoy makes regular exercise more likely. Combining them can also add variety while balancing running’s impact with swimming’s joint friendly resistance.

**1/5** Simple code beats clever code because code is read far more often than it’s written. Saving five minutes today isn’t worth costing every future reader an hour.

**2/5** Clever code makes the reader ask, “How does this work?” Simple code lets them ask the better question: “Does this solve the problem?”

**3/5** Simple code is easier to debug. When something breaks, clear names, straightforward control flow, and small functions help you find the cause without reverse-engineering a puzzle.

**4/5** Simple doesn’t mean simplistic. Some problems are genuinely complex. The goal is to make that complexity visible and manageable—not hide it behind tricks.

**5/5** Write code for the next person who has to change it. That person might be you, six months from now. If they can understand it quickly, that’s clever enough.

1/ Clever code can be satisfying to write. Simple code is easier to read, change, and trust. Most code is read far more often than it is written.

2/ Simple code makes intent visible. Clear names, small functions, and straightforward control flow help the next reader understand what happens without mentally executing every line.

3/ When something breaks, simple code narrows the search. Fewer hidden assumptions and surprising shortcuts mean fewer places for bugs to hide.

4/ Simple does not mean simplistic. A sophisticated algorithm may be necessary, but its implementation can still use clear names, explicit steps, and comments that explain why.

5/ Cleverness has its place. Use it when it solves a real problem, and measure the benefit. Otherwise, choose the version your teammate can understand on a tired Tuesday afternoon.
